story: BAS2012 (2012) is BOLERO-2, a phase 3 randomised trial in 724 women with hormone-receptor-positive advanced breast cancer. studies.title: Alternative rapamycin treatment regimens mitigate the impact of rapamycin on glucose homeostasis and the immune system
studies.finding: Mice given rapamycin every day (2 mg/kg) developed glucose intolerance (the glucose curve was about 71% higher), raised fasting glucose and insulin, and their pancreatic islets released less insulin. The same dose given once every 5 days did not impair glucose tolerance or insulin tolerance, and fasting glucose and insulin stayed normal. Dosing every 3 days was already too frequent. Pyruvate tolerance, a liver measure, was still impaired, about half as much as with daily dosing. The drug is cleared within about a week (blood half-life roughly 15 hours), so mTORC1 was not blocked continuously. studies.title: Intermittent Administration of Rapamycin Extends the Life Span of Female C57BL/6J Mice
studies.journal: The journals of gerontology. Series A, Biological sciences and medical sciences
studies.finding:
Female C57BL/6J mice that started rapamycin at 20 months of age, 2 mg/kg once every 5 days, lived longer than control females. This is the schedule that the same group had earlier shown to have a smaller effect on glucose tolerance and T cells than daily dosing (ARR2015), so the authors argue that rapamycin's effect on lifespan can be separated from many of its side effects.
Boundary: this record rests on the abstract only. The size of the lifespan gain, any male data and any side-effect measurements in these old mice are not extracted yet. The separation claim comes from combining two mouse studies (ARR2015 used young males), not from a single experiment.

studies.title: Restriction of individual branched-chain amino acids has distinct effects on the development and progression of Alzheimer's disease in 3xTg mice
studies.finding: UPDATE (was bioRxiv preprint at seed time, peer-reviewed and published in Advanced Science March 2026). Restricting individual branched-chain amino acids has distinct, sex-specific effects on cognition and AD pathology in 3xTg mice; restriction of isoleucine and valine (but not leucine) promotes metabolic health. studies.finding: A safety-first pilot RCT (n=25, ages 70-95) asking the basic question before any longevity trial: is daily rapamycin safe in healthy older people? Over 8+ weeks it was well tolerated with only minor red-blood-cell changes and - importantly - NO rise in blood glucose or insulin resistance in this short window. Groundwork for larger aging trials like PEARL.

story: Halvor Ullern was first author of the Atlas study ULL2026 in Autophagy Reports. It used kidney cancer cells from patients with Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome, who lack the FLCN gene. Without FLCN, TFEB stays in the nucleus and mTORC1 is overactive, yet general autophagy and LC3 lipidation are not changed. Even so, the autophagy receptor p62 (SQSTM1) collects in enlarged puncta, and the same was seen in kidney tumours from a Norwegian patient group. So p62 build-up can happen without a general autophagy failure. PubMed lists Ullern at the University of Oslo.

highlights.ULL2026: First author: reported that FLCN loss causes p62 accumulation even though bulk autophagy flux stays normal.

pubmed_affiliation: Department of Molecular Medicine, Institute of Basic Medical Sciences, University of Oslo, Oslo, Norway.

studies.title: FLCN loss is characterized by SQSTM1/p62 accumulation despite functional autophagy flux in Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome-associated kidney cancer
studies.finding: In BHD patient-derived kidney cancer cells, FLCN loss causes constitutive nuclear TFEB localization and mTORC1 hyperactivation, but leaves bulk autophagy flux and LC3 lipidation unaffected; however, the autophagy receptor SQSTM1/p62 accumulates in enlarged puncta, a finding replicated in a Norwegian cohort of BHD patient kidney tumors, showing p62 accumulation is dissociable from bulk autophagic flux.

Together they show that rapamycin extended lifespan in mice, including when fed late in life, with a bigger effect in females and at higher doses, while resveratrol and simvastatin did not change lifespan. It shares two co-authors with the Atlas studies, Javors and Strong, both Interventions Testing Program authors.

story: Brian M Castellano was first author of a 2017 paper in Science. PubMed lists the author in the Department of Molecular and Cell Biology at the University of California, Berkeley.

The study showed that cholesterol inside the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment, is a signal that helps switch on mTORC1. A protein called SLC38A9 is needed for this, and it works separately from its role in sensing the amino acid arginine. Another protein, NPC1, which moves cholesterol out of the lysosome, binds SLC38A9 and holds mTORC1 back. The work was done in cultured cells.

highlights.CAS2017: First author of the study showing that lysosomal cholesterol activates mTORC1 through SLC38A9 and NPC1.

pubmed_affiliation: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California at Berkeley, Berkeley, CA 94720, USA.

studies.title: Lysosomal cholesterol activates mTORC1 via an SLC38A9-Niemann-Pick C1 signaling complex
studies.finding: Establishes lysosomal cholesterol as a nutrient input that drives mTORC1 recruitment and activation at the lysosomal surface. SLC38A9 is required for cholesterol-driven mTORC1 activation through conserved cholesterol-responsive motifs, and does so independently of its arginine-sensing function; NPC1, which exports cholesterol from the lysosome, binds SLC38A9 and restrains mTORC1 through its sterol transport function. Boundary: cell lines and patient-derived fibroblasts, no organismal endpoint.

The 2017 paper showed that cholesterol in the lysosome activates mTORC1 through SLC38A9. The 2022 paper identified LYCHOS, a lysosomal protein that senses cholesterol and passes the signal on by holding back the GATOR1 complex.

studies.title: Lysosomal cholesterol activates mTORC1 via an SLC38A9-Niemann-Pick C1 signaling complex
studies.finding: Establishes lysosomal cholesterol as a nutrient input that drives mTORC1 recruitment and activation at the lysosomal surface. SLC38A9 is required for cholesterol-driven mTORC1 activation through conserved cholesterol-responsive motifs, and does so independently of its arginine-sensing function; NPC1, which exports cholesterol from the lysosome, binds SLC38A9 and restrains mTORC1 through its sterol transport function. Boundary: cell lines and patient-derived fibroblasts, no organismal endpoint.

studies.title: Lysosomal GPCR-like protein LYCHOS signals cholesterol sufficiency to mTORC1
studies.finding: Identifies LYCHOS (previously annotated GPR155) as a lysosomal cholesterol sensor for mTORC1. Cholesterol binds the amino-terminal permease-like region; mutating that site impairs mTORC1 activation. At high cholesterol LYCHOS binds GATOR1 through a conserved cytoplasm-facing loop, and by sequestering GATOR1 it promotes cholesterol- and Rag-dependent recruitment of mTORC1 to the lysosome. Boundary: human cell lines and biochemistry, not an organismal phenotype.

story: Ofer Moldavski is a co-author on two papers from the Department of Molecular and Cell Biology at the University of California, Berkeley. He is third author on the 2017 paper and a middle author on the 2018 one.

The 2017 paper showed that lysosomal cholesterol activates mTORC1 through SLC38A9. The 2018 paper described a switch in the Rag-Ragulator scaffold on the lysosome whose grip on mTORC1 changes with nutrient levels. Both are cell studies.

highlights.CAS2017: Third author of the study showing lysosomal cholesterol activates mTORC1 via SLC38A9.
highlights.LAW2018: Middle author of the study on a nutrient-controlled affinity switch in the Rag-Ragulator scaffold.

pubmed_affiliation: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California at Berkeley, Berkeley, CA, USA.

studies.title: Lysosomal cholesterol activates mTORC1 via an SLC38A9-Niemann-Pick C1 signaling complex
studies.finding: Establishes lysosomal cholesterol as a nutrient input that drives mTORC1 recruitment and activation at the lysosomal surface. SLC38A9 is required for cholesterol-driven mTORC1 activation through conserved cholesterol-responsive motifs, and does so independently of its arginine-sensing function; NPC1, which exports cholesterol from the lysosome, binds SLC38A9 and restrains mTORC1 through its sterol transport function. Boundary: cell lines and patient-derived fibroblasts, no organismal endpoint.

studies.finding: A nutrient-induced affinity switch in the Rag-Ragulator scaffold controls mTORC1 lysosomal recruitment.

story: Daniel K Nomura is a middle author on two Science papers from the Department of Molecular and Cell Biology at the University of California, Berkeley. Both are about cholesterol as a signal to mTORC1 in cultured cells.

The 2017 paper showed that cholesterol in the lysosome activates mTORC1 through SLC38A9. The 2022 paper identified LYCHOS, a lysosomal protein that senses cholesterol and holds back the GATOR1 complex.

highlights.SHI2022: Middle author of the study identifying LYCHOS as a lysosomal cholesterol sensor for mTORC1.

studies.title: Lysosomal GPCR-like protein LYCHOS signals cholesterol sufficiency to mTORC1
studies.finding: Identifies LYCHOS (previously annotated GPR155) as a lysosomal cholesterol sensor for mTORC1. Cholesterol binds the amino-terminal permease-like region; mutating that site impairs mTORC1 activation. At high cholesterol LYCHOS binds GATOR1 through a conserved cytoplasm-facing loop, and by sequestering GATOR1 it promotes cholesterol- and Rag-dependent recruitment of mTORC1 to the lysosome. Boundary: human cell lines and biochemistry, not an organismal phenotype.

story: Do Jin Kim appears as a middle author on three Atlas papers from Berkeley, all about how mTORC1 is brought to the lysosome. In 2017 the group solved the structure of the Ragulator complex bound to the Rag proteins (SUX2017). In 2018 they showed that nutrients loosen the Rag-Ragulator grip so the Rags cycle on and off (LAW2018). In 2019 they published the structure of the folliculin complex, which acts as a checkpoint on Rag activation (LAW2019).
PubMed lists the author in the Department of Molecular and Cell Biology at the University of California, Berkeley, on all three papers.

story: Hijai R. Shin was first author of the 2022 Science paper in the Atlas, with Roberto Zoncu as last author. PubMed lists the author at the Department of Molecular and Cell Biology of the University of California, Berkeley.

The team found that a lysosomal protein called LYCHOS binds cholesterol. When cholesterol is high, LYCHOS holds on to the GATOR1 complex, which frees mTORC1 to move to the lysosome and switch on. Changing the cholesterol-binding site weakened mTORC1 activation. The work was done in cells.

highlights.SHI2022: First author: identified LYCHOS as a cholesterol sensor that connects to GATOR1 and mTORC1 at the lysosome.

story: Ming-Yuan Su was first author of a 2017 structural paper in the Atlas from the groups of James H. Hurley and Roberto Zoncu. PubMed lists the author at the Department of Molecular and Cell Biology and the California Institute for Quantitative Biosciences at the University of California, Berkeley.
The team solved the crystal structure of the five-part Ragulator complex and used electron microscopy to model how it presents the RagA/C pair, which recruits mTORC1 to the lysosome.

story: Breanne Sparta was first author of a 2023 paper in the Atlas, with John G. Albeck among the authors. PubMed lists the author at the Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology of the University of California, Davis.

The team followed single human breast-line cells (MCF10A) under the microscope. mTORC1 and TFEB signalling adjusted continuously to amino acids and insulin, and at normal amino acid levels TFEB, AMPK and AKT activity rose and fell together. These changes tracked how fast cells made protein.

highlights.SPA2023: First author of the live-imaging study of continuous nutrient and growth factor sensing by mTORC1-TFEB.

pubmed_affiliation: Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology, University of California, Davis, Davis, United States

studies.title: Continuous sensing of nutrients and growth factors by the mTORC1-TFEB axis
studies.finding: Live imaging of single MCF10A cells shows mTORC1-TFEB signalling adjusts continuously to amino acids and insulin, given alone, one after another or together; at physiological amino acid levels TFEB, AMPK and AKT activity fluctuate in step, and these graded changes track protein synthesis rate through a distributed set of mTORC1 effectors.
